overview.text: Rossini’s *Guillaume Tell* (*William Tell*) is a four-act opera first performed in Paris on August 3, 1829; its French libretto, by Étienne de Jouy and Hippolyte Bis, adapts Friedrich Schiller’s play. The drama presents Tell as a Swiss resister of Habsburg rule: Governor Gesler forces him to shoot an apple from his son Jemmy’s head, and the conflict grows into a struggle for liberty. The opera turns a national-liberation story into large-scale musical drama. It was Rossini’s final opera, and its politically charged subject and vivid orchestral writing—including a famous galloping passage in the overture—help make it distinctive.

key_facts.text: The opera’s French title is *Guillaume Tell*; *William Tell* is its English title.
It premiered in Paris on August 3, 1829, as an opera in four acts.
Its French libretto adapts Friedrich Schiller’s play *Wilhelm Tell*.
In the opera’s story, Governor Gesler tests Tell by making him shoot an apple from Jemmy’s head.
It was Rossini’s final opera; the overture begins with five solo cellos and includes a famous march-gallop.
